newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: ARGENTINE WIND ENERGY PICKS UP, BUT LAWS REQUIRED.
newsitem.headline: ARGENTINE WIND ENERGY PICKS UP, BUT LAWS REQUIRED.

text.p: Argentina will more than triple its wind-generated power capacity this year but legislation is needed to promote the development of this clean energy using the nation's favorable weather and landscape.
"Total wind power in Argentina this year will grow by 7950 kilowatts, or 261 percent," Greenpeace energy campaign director Juan Carlos Villalonga said Wednesday.
"We have one of the world's best conditions for wind energy, but a legal framework is necessary to make sure the industry takes off, attracting private investors."

Powerful winds sweep Argentine barren South Atlantic coast in Patagonia. And in tamer Buenos Aires province, resting just above, winds match those of Germany, Denmark or Holland where this renewable form of energy is highly developed.

Greenpeace noted local legislation is strongly biased towards nuclear and thermo-electric energy, while wind power is hampered by a lack of credit and price distortions. "The widespread use of non-renewable resources which contaminate, like natural gas, has dramatically lowered prices and created distortions that work against wind energy," Villalonga said.

Greenpeace backs a bill that would guarantee wind farms would be able to sell energy not used by the communities they serve to the national electricity grid. They also want deferrals of value-added-tax and incentives for clean energy, like a $0.1 refund per KW of wind power.

Hector Mattio, head of Patagonia's CREE wind energy center, says several projects have fallen through due to lack of financing or the fact investors must pay 21 percent VAT as a lump sum when they collect imported parts at the airport.
"If the law proposed by Greenpeace is approved, there is a good chance we will see very strong growth of wind-generated energy in Argentina," Mattio said.

He noted in Comodoro Rivadavia, 1,100 km south of Buenos Aires, Latin America's largest wind farm is going up with an annual output of 25 million KW. The local cooperative that runs the farm bought eight 750-KW turbines, the most powerful in Argentina, from the Danish firm Micon. They will be in full working order by the end of August, serving 7,000 homes.
The turbines required an investment of $5.3 million pesos and were financed up to 85 percent by Micon. Two other 250-KW turbines set up there in 1995 have set world output records.
Also by year-end three turbines will be built in Buenos Aires province for a total of 40 in Argentina.
The Comodoro Rivadavia farm will prevent the burning of 6.5 million cubic meters of natural gas per year, or 5,520 tonnes of oil, which releases 24,068 tonnes of carbon dioxide.
